analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to sell an increasing share of zero-emission vehicles, reaching 100% by 2035.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with one cosponsor, it sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to force a nationwide switch to zero-emission cars. Starting with model year 2027, each carmaker would have to make sure a rising percentage of the vehicles it sells are zero-emission — 43% in 2027, climbing yearly to 100% in 2035, after which only zero-emission passenger cars could be made or sold. Carmakers that fall short would have to buy credits from those that sell more electric vehicles, or pay civil penalties that go into the Highway Trust Fund. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe air pollution from cars and trucks — the bill's findings say current vehicle soot and smog cause thousands of premature deaths and millions of serious illnesses every year — plus drivers who would benefit as electric vehicle choices, charging infrastructure, and used-car supply expand. Manufacturers that already lead in electric vehicles, such as Tesla, could sell compliance credits to competitors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to vehicle air pollution

how_it_helps.text: The bill's own findings state that zero-emission vehicles would eliminate soot and smog emissions that currently cause thousands of premature deaths and millions of serious illnesses every year in the United States.

Transportation is the largest source of US greenhouse gas emissions, and the bill sets a binding sales schedule for zero-emission vehicles to cut that pollution, culminating in a 100% requirement by model year 2035.

Manufacturers that miss the required percentage of zero-emission sales must pay a civil penalty equal to twice the value of the credits they failed to submit, with the money deposited into the Highway Trust Fund.
The bill preserves states' authority to set their own zero-emission vehicle requirements, so states can go further than the federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Car manufacturers, especially those slow to electrify, who would face rising compliance costs, credit purchases, or penalties; and to some extent car buyers, if manufacturers pass along the cost of the transition or if electric models cost more than the gas cars they replace.

drawbacks.text: The mandate rides on a single technology path: after 2035, the EPA must enjoin the manufacture of any passenger vehicle other than a zero-emission vehicle, regardless of how affordable the vehicles or how ready the charging and grid infrastructure are at that point.

A tradeable credit market lets manufacturers that miss targets buy their way into compliance rather than sell more zero-emission vehicles — a structure under which, in California's similar program, leading electric-car makers have earned billions selling credits to legacy automakers while fleet turnover lagged.

Manufacturers face civil penalties at twice the value of missing credits, costs that could be passed to car buyers, and the bill does not include direct consumer affordability measures such as purchase subsidies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and climate case is strong and the credit-trading design gives industry flexibility, but the hard 2035 cutoff and reliance on credits rather than direct sales could slow actual fleet turnover and raise car prices in the interim. A better-designed version would pair the mandate with stronger affordability and charging investments.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended, so it never reached the floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Zero-Emission Vehicles Act of 2024 on February 29, 2024, joined by Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse as its sole cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
That referral was the bill's final action; the Congress ended January 3, 2025, with no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers that wanted to keep selling gasoline vehicles without a federal deadline, and the gasoline industry, since no sales mandate was ever enacted; no one in Congress had to vote on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Carmakers and oil, which faced no mandate

sides.party_line_note: The bill's supporters were both Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it, and the Democratic-run committee that could have moved it took no action.

industries.note: The bill forces a full sales transition to zero-emission vehicles by 2035, penalizing manufacturers that lag and creating a credit market that rewards early EV leaders like Tesla while raising costs for laggards. Automakers opposed binding sales mandates, arguing technology and consumer demand were not ready.
A full shift of new-car sales to electric would steadily shrink gasoline demand, the industry's core retail market. The industry's interest ran against the bill's public health and climate goals.

A guaranteed growing share of zero-emission sales plus a tradeable credit market creates a revenue stream for makers of electric vehicles and their batteries. Early leaders could sell credits to competitors for profit.
A binding national sales schedule gives charging companies certainty to invest, one of the benefits the bill's findings cite explicitly.
